title: Learnable quantum spectral filters for hybrid graph neural networks

affiliation.name: Istanbul Medeniyet University

papers.abstract: In this paper, we describe a parameterized quantum circuit that can be considered as convolutional and pooling layers for graph neural networks. The circuit incorporates the parameterized quantum Fourier circuit where the qubit connections for the controlled gates derived from the Laplacian operator. Specifically, we show that the eigenspace of the Laplacian operator of a graph can be approximated by using QFT based circuit whose connections are determined from the adjacency matrix. For an N × N Laplacian, this approach yields an approximate polynomial-depth circuit requiring only n = log(N) qubits. These types of circuits can eliminate the expensive classical computations for approximating the learnable functions of the Laplacian through Chebyshev polynomial or Taylor expansions. Using this circuit as a convolutional layer provides an n− dimensional probability vector that can be considered as the filtered and compressed graph signal. Therefore, the circuit along with the measurement can be considered a very efficient convolution plus pooling layer that transforms an N-dimensional signal input into n−dimensional signal with an exponential compression. We then apply a classical neural network prediction head to the output of the circuit to construct a complete graph neural network. Since the circuit incorporates geometric structure through its graph connection-based approach, we present graph classification results for the benchmark datasets listed in TUDataset library (AIDS, Letter-high, Letter-med, Letter-low, MUTAG, ENZYMES, PROTEINS, COX2, BZR, DHFR, MSRC-9). Using only [1-100] learnable parameters for the quantum circuit and minimal classical layers (1000-5000 parameters) in a generic setting, the obtained results are comparable to and in some cases better than many of the baseline results, particularly for the cases when geometric structure plays a significant role.

title: HyHO-DDI: A Hypergraph Neural Network for High-Order Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Objective: Drug–drug interactions (DDIs) are a major cause of adverse drug reactions (ADRs), particularly in patients receiving multiple medications. Existing computational methods predominantly focus on pairwise interactions, limiting their ability to capture the complex effects of high-order (multi-drug) therapies. This study proposes a computational framework for predicting myopathy-associated high-order DDIs.Methods: We propose HyHO-DDIs, a hypergraph neural network model for predicting myopathy-associated high-order drug combinations using a dataset curated from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). In our model, each drug is represented by molecular fingerprint features and a protein-target profile, and we construct a hypergraph in which nodes are drugs and hyperedges correspond to multi-drug combinations implicated in myopathy. The model integrates Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) layers with hypergraph-based attention to learn high-order interaction representations, and a decoder outputs the predicted risk of myopathy for an input drug combination. We evaluated HyHO-DDI with 5-fold cross-validation and compared it against an MLP with the same inputs, as well as established high-order baselines (HODDI, D3I).Results: HyHO-DDI consistently achieved higher performance across F1-score, AUROC, and AUC-PR. The proposed model reduced false-positive predictions while maintaining strong performance on previously unseen drug combinations, demonstrating robust generalization.Conclusion: HyHO-DDI provides an effective framework for predicting myopathy-associated high-order DDIs by explicitly modeling multi-drug interactions with hypergraphs. The proposed approach has the potential to improve computational pharmacovigilance by prioritizing potentially hazardous drug combinations and supporting medication safety.</jats:p>

title: Prediction of Supercritical CO₂ Solubility with a Thermodynamics-Conditioned Equivariant Graph Neural Network Model
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Supercritical CO₂ (scCO₂) is a green alternative to organic solvents and the working fluid of supercritical fluid extraction (SFE), used in analytical sample preparation and natural-product isolation. Its wider adoption is limited by the difficulty of predicting analyte solubility: experimental determination at supercritical conditions is tedious, requires specialized equipment, and yields values that vary by up to two orders of magnitude across laboratories. Existing predictive models either rely on substance-specific fitted parameters or trade mechanistic transparency for accuracy. We present an interpretable graph-neural-network framework that couples the equivariant Polarizable Atom Interaction Neural Network (PaiNN) with Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), integrating global thermodynamic descriptors (temperature, pressure, density, evaporation enthalpy, critical point) into a three-dimensional structure-aware model. It was trained on 27,461 solubility measurements across 958 organic molecules curated from Makarov et al., 2025. Five-fold cross-validation gave a coefficient of determination of 0.767 and a median absolute deviation of 0.36 in log₁₀-solubility, with stable per-fold performance (R² = 0.767 ± 0.048) and confirmation on an external dataset. To verify the model reasons chemically, we adapted a walk-based GNN layer-wise relevance propagation explainer to the FiLM architecture and added structural ablation. Atom-rank consistency across folds (ρ = 0.72), plausible element rankings (O, N > C, H), and trends with molecular weight, polar surface area and acetylation show that predictions rest on physically meaningful patterns. The ready-to-use model enables in silico SFE screening and reduces organic-solvent use in sample preparation.</jats:p>

title: Cross-Attention Gradient Transplantation (CAGT): Mitigating Gradient Conflict in Multi-Task Learning Through Cross-Blockwise Attention
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Multi-task learning tries to use shared structure across tasks that are related by optimizing a joint objective. In practice though, gradients from individual tasks losses can cause conflict. This causes destructive interference that slows convergence and reduces performance. Previous approaches like PCGrad and CAGrad address this by projecting away or reweighting conflicting gradients at the vector level, but they do not explicitly exchange or reuse gradient components across tasks. This paper proposes Cross-Attention Gradient Transplantation (CAGT), which is a method that finds conflicting gradient components and replaces them using deterministic cosine similarity based cross-attention over gradient subblocks from other tasks. Task gradients are partitioned into subblocks at each optimization step, and for each subblock showing conflict, attention weights are computed from cosine similarities with other tasks' subblocks. The resulting weighted combination is rescaled to keep the original magnitude, and it is interpolated with the original subgradient. This produces adjusted task gradients that reduce adversarial interactions while keeping constructive signals. Experimental results show that CAGT outperforms traditional approaches such as PCGrad and CAGrad, achieving roughly 10% lower loss values on some multi task datasets, such as ROT-MNIST and CelebA.</jats:p>

title: Proactive Gradient Conflict Mitigation in Multi-Task Learning:A Sparse Training Perspective
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Advancing towards generalist agents necessitates the concurrent processing of multiple tasks using a unified model, thereby underscoring the growing significance of simultaneous model training on multiple downstream tasks. A common issue in multi-task learning is the occurrence of gradient conflict, which leads to potential competition among different tasks during joint training. This competition often results in improvements in one task at the expense of deterioration in another. Although several optimization methods have been developed to address this issue by manipulating task gradients for better task balancing, they cannot decrease the incidence of gradient conflict. In this paper, we systematically investigate the occurrence of gradient conflict across different methods and propose a strategy to reduce such conflicts through sparse training (ST), wherein only a portion of the model’s parameters are updated during training while keeping the rest unchanged. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that ST effectively mitigates conflicting gradients and leads to superior performance. Furthermore, ST can be easily integrated with gradient manipulation techniques, thus enhancing their effectiveness.</jats:p>

title: Adaptive Gradient Balancing Strategy for Multi-Task Optimization in Visual Recognition Systems
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Multi-task learning enables neural networks to address multiple related problems through shared representations, yet practical deployment remains hindered by gradient conflicts arising from heterogeneous task objectives that cause negative transfer during optimization. This work introduces an adaptive gradient balancing framework that addresses these challenges through principled integration of conflict detection and dynamic weight adjustment. The proposed method employs a gradient similarity metric to quantify inter-task interference by analyzing geometric alignment of task-specific gradients in parameter space, then translates conflict measurements into adaptive importance coefficients via an exponential moving average scheme that responds to both gradient disagreement intensity and task-specific loss reduction rates. Theoretical analysis establishes convergence guarantees under standard smoothness assumptions, demonstrating that the framework produces gradient updates with bounded variance comparable to conventional stochastic gradient descent. Extensive experiments on NYU Depth V2, Cityscapes, and PASCAL-Context benchmarks validate the approach across diverse task combinations spanning semantic segmentation, depth estimation, surface normal prediction, instance segmentation, and edge detection. Results demonstrate consistent improvements over eight state-of-the-art baselines, achieving 42.3% mIoU on NYU Depth V2 semantic segmentation with only 8.3% computational overhead while converging 1.8 times faster than competing methods. Visualization analyses reveal interpretable weight evolution patterns where the mechanism dynamically allocates optimization focus based on training dynamics, ultimately guiding tasks toward harmonious gradient alignment rather than persistent interference.</jats:p>

title: Variable multi-scale attention fusion network and adaptive correcting gradient optimization for multi-task learning
Computational Optimization Nash-MTL: An Efficient Multi-Task Learning Method Based on Gradient Intelligent Sampling
container-title: Science and Technology of Engineering, Chemistry and Environmental Protection
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Aiming at the exponential computational complexity problem of Nash-MTL in multi-task learning, this paper proposes a computationally optimized Nash-MTL framework. This method introduces three core points. First, there is a phased gradient update mechanism, which combines cyclic sampling and dynamic random sampling strategies, and can maintain the optimized performance while To minimize redundant gradient computing, secondly, there is a dynamic importance scheduling model, which assesses task priority by means of loss change rate and gradient size, thereby intelligently allocating computing resources, and is also supplemented by a security recovery strategy. Thirdly, there is a stability guarantee mechanism with periodic global updates and abnormal trigger rollback operations. Experiments were conducted on QM9, NYUv2 and cityscape datasets, which confirmed the effectiveness of the framework. The framework can maintain task performance (with a deviation within 5%) while significantly reducing computing time by 55.4%. These advancements greatly enhance the feasibility of deploying complex multi-task learning systems in resource-constrained edge computing environments.</jats:p>
